//: Scope config for acceptance/test-repo-standard.mjs, the committed repo-hygiene lint.
//about: The CANON (six Keep a Changelog categories, standard-readme structure with License last, the voice ban) is hardcoded in the lint; this file tunes SCOPE only. Keys starting with // are operator comments; unknown keys are hard errors. Deleting this file still runs the full canon, but with the lint's laxer built-in scope (no counts, no extra sections, minSections 1). This shipped file IS the stricter house default.
//docs: Paths of the governed meta docs. 'extra' adds more files to the voice/count sweeps. An INDEX is the catalog a directory keeps of itself: 'index' declares one, 'indexes' a list, never both, and both normalise to the same list. { "file": "acceptance/README.md", "extensions": [".mjs"], "scope": "direct", "statuses": true, "aliases": { "HONEST-ARTIFACT": "reference" }, "ordered": true, "reconciled": true, "requireDate": false, "ignore": [...] }. RS-index holds coverage (every file the index speaks for has a row), resolution (every row points at a file that exists), containment (no row reaches outside the directory), uniqueness (no file catalogued twice), and the shape of each row; it cannot hold whether a description is still true. 'file' must sit inside the directory it catalogues, and must also appear in 'extra', because an index no prose sweep reaches is the one page in its directory that can rot with nothing here noticing. 'extensions' defaults to [".md"], so an index over engines is just [".mjs"]; ["*"] means every kept file the directory holds, and it is the only selector that reaches a Dockerfile, a Makefile, or an extensionless script, so it is the only one that can promise complete coverage. 'scope' is "recursive" (the default, and what every pre-0.8 config means) or "direct" (this index owns the files directly in its directory, and a nested directory keeps its own); either way OWNERSHIP IS PER FILE: a file's owner is the deepest declaration that actually claims it, so a declared child bounds its ancestor over the files that child CLAIMS rather than over its whole directory, nesting never needs a hand-written 'ignore', and a file the child does not speak for stays the parent's. An index is a declaration rather than content, so no index catalogues another. A kept file no declaration claims is UNDECIDED, named in a skip rather than failed on, because a repo indexing its markdown and not its images has said what it wanted; what it may never be is silent. 'statuses' is OFF until declared (true = the whole canon) and prints a named skip while off; the words are CANON (active, superseded, reference, design, delivered) in whatever case the page writes them, matched by the word a cell BEGINS with, and a genuinely different word keeps its place on the page through 'aliases'. 'ordered' is OFF until declared and prints a named skip while off: with it on, rows must sit in ascending path order, which is the only order a later sweep reproduces, so the next run over the directory produces a diff instead of a rewrite. Dates: 'reconciled' wants ONE line, "Reconciled against the code: YYYY-MM-DD", for the whole directory; 'requireDate' wants one per row and is OFF by default, because an index recording no dates is an honest shape and inventing them is the one outcome this check exists to prevent. Neither set prints a named skip. The lint checks the line exists and is well formed, never how old it is: a verdict that changes overnight is the calendar dependence this standard rejects everywhere else. The file universe is what git tracks plus what it does not ignore, so a build directory owes no rows; it is read NUL-delimited because git quotes any path outside plain ASCII and a filename can contain a newline, a symlink owes a row and is reported as a symlink rather than read through, and a submodule owes nothing. Without git nothing is excluded, which demands more rows rather than fewer. 'grammar' is 1 (the default) or 2 and decides how the page is PARSED: under 1 any line starting with | is a candidate row and any cell answers for anything, so an unrelated table whose rows link files counts as coverage, a description beginning with a status word satisfies the status rule while the status column is empty, and a date in any column answers for a blank verification column (the gate prints RS-index (grammar) naming exactly that); under 2 a catalog row is a body row of a table whose HEADER names a file column, the status is read from the status column and the date from the column that says when the file was last checked. 1 is the default because changing what a row MEANS under an existing adopter is a migration rather than a fix. A table inside a code fence is an example under BOTH and its rows are never coverage. 'retain' records that this index STAYS where it is rather than moving to the README a reader lands on, carries the reason like every other recorded no, and prints as a named skip: without it the offer returned on every run and a decision somebody had made looked exactly like one nobody had.
//docs.declined: Directories that were OFFERED an index and turned it down, one { dir, why } each. The reason is required: a recorded no with no reason is indistinguishable from an oversight, and the next person to read this config is the one who has to tell them apart. This exists at directory granularity because the alternative is a repo-wide 'never ask about indexes again', which suppresses the directories that matter along with the leaf nobody wants catalogued. Each entry prints as a named skip on every run, so a decline is visible rather than silent.
//docs.ownership: How much of the repo the index rules may stay SILENT about. "declared" (the default, and what every config written before this key means) holds each index to the files its own declaration reaches: a Dockerfile beside an index declared over .mjs is named in a skip and the build stays green, because an extension list is the operator's answer and reddening it would impose a scope nobody gave. "strict" makes the undecided set the VERDICT: every kept file under a declared index owes exactly one owner, an 'ignore' entry, or a 'docs.declined' record, and every directory holding kept files that no declaration reaches fails until somebody answers for it. Only under "strict" is "a file added tomorrow reddens the build" a sentence this standard keeps, and strict enforces the same way BEFORE the first index exists: a repo declaring it with zero declarations is a repo where nothing is owned by anything. Two sets of files sit outside the model in both modes and are NAMED rather than passed: a file at the repo root (no declaration can reach one, because an index lives inside the directory it catalogues) and a file under a dot-directory (excluded the way assets.coverage excludes one; declare an index for it to bring it in). Under strict the gate prints RS-index (ownership boundary) with the count and the paths on every run, because a silent exclusion reads exactly like coverage. It is opt-in because adopting it is a migration rather than a fix: turn it on once the atlas is complete, not on upgrade.
//manifest: A provenance/inventory doc whose Totals line must reconcile with its own table rows, e.g. { "file": "COPY-MANIFEST.md", "statuses": ["UNCHANGED", "MODIFIED", "NEW"] }. false = this repo has none (the check prints SKIP, never a silent pass).
//versionManifest: Where the released version lives, for the CHANGELOG lockstep. Omit to auto-detect (.claude-plugin/plugin.json, then package.json); a path string for a JSON manifest with .version; { "file": ..., "match": "regex with one capture" } for non-JSON; false if the repo has no version manifest.
//readme: requireSections: extra required README sections beyond the hardcoded canon, as case-insensitive regexes over H2 headings. docsOnly: standard-readme's own documentation-repository exception. Set true ONLY for a repo with no functional code; it waives Install + Usage and nothing else (default false).
//conventions: The `## N.` contiguity rule is hardcoded; minSections is an anti-gutting floor.
//voice: extraBanned appends to the hardcoded marketing-ban list (each extra term must also be documented in CONVENTIONS, which the reflexivity check enforces). properNouns: exact, CASE-SENSITIVE names exempt from the ban, for a product genuinely called e.g. 'Seamless Deploy'. Every active exemption prints on every run, so it can never hide. alsoScan widens the sweep to more files.
//counts: Machine-checked numeric claims, keyed by a stable id. Each: pattern (regex, group 1 captures the number), and a source of truth: glob (literal dirs + '*' in the basename only), or file+lineRegex, or neither for cross-doc-agreement-only numbers. Optional: docs (which docs to scan; default the whole meta-doc set), minMentions (the claim must appear at least N times), and under (a regex over heading text: scan only that section, so a historical number in a dated CHANGELOG release block stays history instead of failing forever once the live count moves). Declare a count ONLY when the repo actually states it in prose.
//stableDocs: Rarely-changing meta files that must exist and open with an H1. Replacing this list is a visible weakening, so think before shrinking it.
//prose: The enterprise writing profile, off by default because prose style is a house choice and switching it on mid-life reddens a repo's whole back catalogue at once. Adopt it with the voice skill, which sweeps FIRST and locks second: { "profile": "enterprise", "scan": "docs" | "markdown" | "all", "extraBanned": [...], "allow": [{ "term": ..., "why": ... }], "exempt": [{ "path": ..., "why": ... }] }. The two families reach different distances on purpose: dashes go as far as scan says, filler stops at markdown prose (in source, leverageRatio is an identifier rather than register). The word lists are canon and live in the lint; allow lifts one filler term with a printed reason, and the dash rules can never be lifted. Released CHANGELOG history and the license file are out of scope by canon.
//assets: The generated README identity (banners and pills rendered from .github/assets/manifest.json by the generator beside it), off by default. Adopt it with the identity skill, which previews before it writes: { "dir": ".github/assets", "coverage": { "roots": [...], "ignore": [...] } }. coverage makes every immediate subdirectory of a root earn a README, so a new one cannot appear undocumented; it is one level deep per root, so name a nested directory's parent as its own root to police inside it.
//ignore: The trust ruleset's scope. The .env leg is canon and needs no configuration: the whole family is ignored, and only an example file may be re-exposed by a negation. Declare generated paths that must stay ignored AND untracked, plus any extra .env-family example filenames a negation may re-expose. `file` relocates the ignore file being checked, for a repo that keeps its rules somewhere other than .gitignore. This is ignore-rule hygiene; no file contents are ever read.
//github: What this repo recorded as synced to its GitHub About panel, written by the scaffold skill once the operator approved the sync: { "about": { "description": "<the one line, the same claim as the README tagline>", "homepage": "<url>", "topics": [...] } }. false = nothing recorded, and RS-about prints a named skip. Only 'description' is ever re-checked, against the README's own tagline, so the panel cannot quietly describe a repo that has moved on; 'homepage' and 'topics' are recorded provenance, kept so a re-run knows what was applied. Omit 'homepage' when the repo publishes none of its own (null reads as absent; an empty string is a config error rather than a quiet way to record nothing). The lint takes no network, so what GitHub is serving right now is never verified here.
//scaffold: Provenance, written by the scaffold skill and never by hand: { "pluginVersion": "<the plugin version that scaffolded this repo>", "answers": { "<PLACEHOLDER>": "<the value the operator confirmed>" } }. A re-run pre-fills its questions from answers and re-asks only what is missing, and the repo itself can answer which standard version governs it. A declined offer is recorded here too (IDENTITY_OFFER / PROSE_OFFER = declined), so a re-run does not ask again. The lint validates the shape only; enforcement never varies by it.
//checks: The only off switch, per check id, and it is loud: { "<id>": { "enabled": false, "why": "<reason printed on every run>" } }. Ids: changelog, lockstep, readme, conventions, manifest, voice, prose, counts, reflexivity, stable-docs, todos, license, placeholders, shadow, assets, ignore, index, about.
